title: With Due Respect (Vol. 1) -- Ch. 1: GMA's Legacy
keywords: without trust, no leader can succeed
the things that money cannot buy
primary_topics: Chapter 1 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 1) -- CJP's August 12, 2007 Philippine Daily Inquirer column asking how President Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo (GMA) will be remembered, and whether her State of the Nation Address (SONA) legacy of infrastructure, a social safety net, and peace in Mindanao is achievable

His central argument that the President's first priority is not funding her 'grandiose dreams' but earning the people's trust -- 'without trust, no leader can succeed' -- paraphrasing Salonga that the things money cannot buy (integrity, public esteem, character, moral ascendancy, credibility) matter more than the roads and bridges money can buy

Two credibility-building prescriptions that 'require no funding': (1) leading an internal transformation by holding relatives, officials and cronies to the Constitution and anti-graft, ethics and procurement laws -- being 'transformational, no longer transactional'; and (2) fortifying democratic institutions by naming trustworthy appointees to the Supreme Court and Comelec

A pointed warning against packing the courts with 'loyalists' -- invoking Eisenhower (whose choices Warren and Brennan voted against him) and Marcos (whose compliant Court aggravated the discontent that toppled him) -- and the assurance that 'with prudent legal advice, goals can be attained under the rule of law'
sub_topics: GMA's SONA three priorities: investments in physical, intellectual, legal and security infrastructure ('imprastraktura para sa negosyo at trabaho'); a wider safety net (cheap medicine, affordable housing, better schools and teachers, scholarships, English proficiency -- 'dunong at kalusugan ang susi sa kasaganaan'); and peace in Mindanao, crushing terrorism, and ending human-rights abuses
The critics' question -- where will she find 'the trillions to fund her grandiose dreams': borrow again, raise taxes again, or sell the nation's patrimony?

Credibility-first: even with funding, the first priority is to earn the people's trust; CJP cites Cardinal Gaudencio Rosales ('it is treason to lead without a vision, supported by core values') and his own refrain that 'visionary leadership by example is the best way to lead'

The Salonga paraphrase: it is good to aspire for the things money can buy (roads, skyways, bridges, airports, schools, power plants), but better to have first the things money cannot buy -- integrity, public esteem, character, moral ascendancy and credibility

Prescription 1 -- internal transformation: tell relatives, officials and cronies that past wrongs will be set aside, but henceforth they must strictly follow the Constitution, the anti-graft law, the ethical-standards law and procurement laws; lead by example and use presidential strength to be 'transformational, no longer transactional'

Prescription 2 -- fortify institutions: between then and June 30, 2010, eight justices would retire (Garcia, Gutierrez, Reyes, Azcuna, Tinga, Ynares-Santiago, Quisumbing, Chico-Nazario) and Chief Justice Puno's term would end May 17, 2010, so GMA would name all 15 justices and all 7 Comelec commissioners; the Constitution bars appointments in the two months before a presidential election

The anti-court-packing warning: tempted by debacles (EO 464, the 'calibrated preemptive response,' PP 1017, the People's Initiative) to fill the Court with 'loyalists,' she should 'banish the thought' -- Eisenhower's appointees (Warren, Brennan) voted against him, and Marcos's compliant Court 'aggravated the discontent that eventually toppled and disgraced him'

The Comelec angle: with the impending retirements of Chair Abalos and Commissioners Borra and Tuason, GMA could name a credible chair and commissioners (CJP floats names such as Romulo Macalintal, Leila de Lima and Howard Calleja); without credible officials, electoral reform and an orderly 2010 election are illusory

stances.claim: GMA's true first priority is not financing her SONA legacy but earning the people's trust, because 'without trust, no leader can succeed'; and trust is built on 'the things that money cannot buy' -- integrity, public esteem, character, moral ascendancy and credibility -- not on infrastructure alone.
stances.rhetorical_move: things-money-cannot-buy reframing: shifting the legacy debate from funding to credibility by ranking intangible virtues above material works

stances.claim: She should fortify the Supreme Court and the Comelec with trustworthy appointees rather than 'loyalists' -- court-packing backfires, as Eisenhower learned (Warren and Brennan voted against him) and as Marcos learned (a compliant Court aggravated the discontent that toppled him) -- because 'with prudent legal advice, goals can be attained under the rule of law.'
stances.rhetorical_move: cautionary-precedent argument: deploying two historical court-packing failures to show that a captured court is self-defeating

stances.claim: Leading an internal transformation (holding relatives and cronies to the Constitution and anti-graft laws) and fortifying institutions would be 'a lasting legacy that requires no funding' and would itself elevate her credibility -- presidential strength used to be 'transformational, no longer transactional.'
stances.rhetorical_move: costless-legacy framing: presenting integrity reforms as both free and self-reinforcing for credibility

notable_anecdotes: Eisenhower's revenge appointees: CJP recalls that Dwight Eisenhower's own US Supreme Court choices, led by Earl Warren and William Brennan, ended up voting down his cases -- a warning that packing a court with loyalists rarely delivers loyalty.

Marcos's compliant Court: he notes that Ferdinand Marcos produced a pliant Supreme Court that 'ironically' deepened the discontent that 'eventually toppled and disgraced him' -- the cautionary opposite of an independent judiciary.

Naming names for the Comelec: CJP openly floats candidates he considers credible for the vacant Comelec posts -- a chair like Romulo Macalintal and commissioners like Leila de Lima and Howard Calleja -- to show that fortification is concrete, not abstract.

The legacy that costs nothing: against the critics asking where GMA will find 'the trillions,' he argues that transforming her own leadership and fortifying the Court and Comelec 'requires no funding' yet would be her most lasting legacy.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 1 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 1) is CJP's August 12, 2007 Inquirer column asking how President Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo (GMA) will be remembered, and whether her State of the Nation Address legacy -- infrastructure, a wider social safety net, and peace in Mindanao -- is achievable. Granting that her aspirations are hard to fault, he reframes the debate: the critics ask where she will find 'the trillions' to fund them, but the real first priority, he argues, is to earn the people's trust, 'for without trust, no leader can succeed.' Citing Cardinal Rosales ('it is treason to lead without a vision, supported by core values') and paraphrasing Salonga, he insists that beyond the things money can buy (roads, bridges, schools), it is 'the things that money cannot buy' -- integrity, public esteem, character, moral ascendancy and credibility -- that matter most, and GMA's record-low ratings stem from her credibility deficit. He offers two prescriptions that 'require no funding': first, lead an internal transformation by holding relatives, officials and cronies strictly to the Constitution and the anti-graft, ethics and procurement laws, wielding presidential strength to be 'transformational, no longer transactional'; second, fortify democratic institutions by naming trustworthy -- not 'loyalist' -- appointees to the Supreme Court and the Comelec, since between 2007 and 2010 she would fill all fifteen Court seats (eight justices retiring, plus Chief Justice Puno) and all seven Comelec posts. He warns that court-packing backfires, recalling that Eisenhower's appointees Warren and Brennan voted against him and that Marcos's compliant Court 'aggravated the discontent that eventually toppled and disgraced him,' and assures her that 'with prudent legal advice, goals can be attained under the rule of law.' Such selfless acts, he concludes, would be a lasting legacy that costs nothing and would itself lift her credibility -- the key to making her SONA dreams a 2010 reality.
